name: Rome
title: An arena. A ruin. A city that kept going.
deck: The Colosseum survived as its surroundings and purpose changed. Read the city as layers, rather than a single ancient moment.
archiveTitle: Inside the Colosseum
archiveType: Photochrom print · historical colours added in printing
modernTitle: The Colosseum in the present-day city
changed: From an imperial spectacle to an archaeological landmark: the structure remains, but the way people use and understand it has changed.
persisted: The amphitheatre still anchors how visitors recognise Rome. Survival, adaptation, excavation, and conservation all belong to its history.
notice: Look at the exposed interior in the archive print. A familiar monument was already a ruin long before today’s visitor experience.
eras: The amphitheatre belonged to a much wider city of forums, public monuments, infrastructure, and imperial power.
Another city within the old one
Religious and public buildings added new centres of activity alongside the remains of antiquity. Rome did not stop developing when imperial rule changed.
The archive print presents an already ancient monument to an expanding audience for travel images. It documents its own era, not the arena in Roman times.
A living city around an archaeological site
The Colosseum is both a protected monument and part of modern Rome. Its meaning now includes research, conservation, and public access.

name: Istanbul
title: The water stayed. The capital changed.
deck: Read a city shaped by different empires through its enduring maritime setting and its changing skyline.
archiveTitle: The Golden Horn in Constantinople
archiveType: Photochrom print · historical colours added in printing
modernTitle: Galata Bridge across the Golden Horn
changed: Different political and religious centres added new buildings to the skyline. The historic city now sits inside a much larger metropolis.
persisted: The water remains a powerful organising feature. The Golden Horn and Bosphorus still help explain how districts face and connect with one another.
notice: Notice how densely the historic waterfront was already built. The archive is a late Ottoman-era view, not an image of Byzantine Constantinople.
eras: Hagia Sophia became one of the city’s defining monumental buildings, reflecting its role as a major religious and political centre.
Buildings including the Süleymaniye Mosque added another architectural layer. Later power did not erase every trace of earlier urban life.
The historical view records the Golden Horn in the late Ottoman period. The name Constantinople in its catalogue belongs to that archival record.
Historic waterfronts and monuments remain within a growing urban region. The challenge is caring for these layers while everyday city life continues.

name: London
title: One river. Many generations of crossings.
deck: London Bridge offers a thread through a city repeatedly rebuilt around the Thames.
archiveTitle: London Bridge in a late-Victorian print
archiveType: Photochrom print · historical colours added in printing
modernTitle: A present-day view of London Bridge
changed: The bridge in the historical print is not the bridge standing here now. Structures, traffic, and the skyline change even when a crossing keeps its name.
persisted: The Thames crossing remains a useful connection between the banks. A long-lived route need not depend on one long-lived structure.
notice: Compare the bridge forms and their surroundings. These are different bridges and viewpoints, not a perfectly aligned before-and-after pair.

sources.name: UK Parliament · Rebuilding after the Great Fire

eras: A crossing helps make a town
Londinium developed with a bridge, roads, and river trade. The crossing connected movement on land with activity along the Thames.
The Great Fire destroyed much of the City. A rebuilding act followed in 1667, shaping how the damaged city was reconstructed.
This print shows an earlier London Bridge and a working river landscape. Its date matters: it does not depict the medieval bridge or the modern one.
Today’s London Bridge continues a long history of crossing at this part of the Thames, within a markedly changed cityscape.

name: Cairo
title: A city grew beyond its first boundaries.
deck: An archive view from the Nile opens a longer story: a medieval capital became one layer within a much larger urban landscape.
archiveTitle: The Nile shore near Bulaq
archiveType: Historical photochrom view · colour is a printing treatment
modernTitle: A wider view of present-day Cairo
changed: The modern urban landscape extends around older districts and monuments. The archive riverbank view is one fragment of that longer expansion.
persisted: Riverfront activity and long-established neighbourhoods remain part of Cairo’s story. The medieval city is still legible within later urban layers.
notice: The old view documents a working Nile shore. It is not a photograph of medieval Cairo, and it does not show the whole nineteenth-century city.

sources.name: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities · Historical Cairo

eras: The Fatimids founded al-Qahira northeast of earlier settlements. Al-Azhar was commissioned soon afterwards, giving the new city a major institution.
Mosques, schools, fountains, and other buildings contributed to a major urban and cultural centre. Historic Cairo preserves many layers rather than one frozen date.
The archive image shows the Nile shore near Bulaq, including a sailing vessel. It is evidence of a particular riverside scene in a later era.
A historic city inside a metropolis
Older neighbourhoods and monumental buildings coexist with much later growth. A photograph of one district cannot stand for the entire city.

name: Kyoto
title: A capital moved. A cultural city endured.
deck: Kyoto’s story continues after its imperial role changed. Streets, wooden buildings, and cultural practices carry different kinds of continuity.
archiveTitle: Street decorations in Kyoto
archiveType: Hand-coloured albumen photograph · unknown photographer, Rijksmuseum collection
modernTitle: A present-day street in Gion, Kyoto
changed: The political centre shifted, while later infrastructure and modern urban life altered the city. Historic wooden streets survive through continued care, not by being untouched.
persisted: Kyoto retained a strong cultural identity after its imperial role ended. Building traditions and gardens remain important alongside everyday urban change.
notice: Look at the decorated street in the historical photograph. The modern view is another Kyoto street, not a claim that this exact scene survives unchanged.

sources.name: UNESCO · Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto
Kyoto official tourism · History of Kyoto

eras: Heian-kyo was established as a new capital, drawing on Chinese capital planning. It became the setting for a long development of Japanese culture.
Kyoto’s role changed as the imperial centre moved to Tokyo. Losing that political role did not mean losing the city’s cultural life.
This archival photograph documents street decorations. Its hand colouring is part of the historical object, not evidence that the camera captured colour naturally.
Traditional streets, wooden architecture, and gardens exist alongside a modern city. Preservation is an ongoing choice involving buildings and the people who use them.

name: Berlin
title: The gate stayed. The barrier disappeared.
deck: One landmark became a border, then a meeting place. Compare the space around the Brandenburg Gate—not just the stonework.
archiveTitle: The Wall at the Brandenburg Gate
modernTitle: Brandenburg Gate in an open public square
changed: The barrier and restricted ground transformed access to the gate. Their removal changed the meaning and use of the same landmark.
persisted: The gate remained recognisable through division and reopening. Its architectural continuity makes the political change especially visible.
notice: The 1961 photograph records a divided city. Compare restricted space with today’s public access; the images use different viewpoints.

sources.name: Berlin State Monuments Office · Development of the Wall

eras: A landmark with an earlier history
The gate existed long before the Berlin Wall. It had already experienced war damage and restoration.
A gate people could not reach
Construction of the Wall placed the gate within restricted ground. The archive photograph records the barrier that November.
The opening of the Wall transformed the gate into a symbol of unity. The crossing here reopened in December.
The landmark now faces an accessible public setting. Remembering the border gives that openness historical meaning.

name: Singapore
title: From cargo river to civic waterfront.
deck: Boat Quay makes urban transformation visible: the river stayed while work, buildings, and the use of its banks changed.
archiveTitle: Boats at Singapore’s Boat Quay
modernTitle: Boat Quay beside the modern skyline
changed: River cleanup and redevelopment altered waterfront work and land use. Businesses and communities were relocated as part of that transformation.
persisted: The river bend and quays remain a thread between the trading settlement and present-day city.
notice: Look for working boats and waterfront buildings in the archive. The newer image shows a different phase of the river’s urban role.

sources.name: National Library Board · Singapore’s Waterfront Life
National Library Board · Nature and Environment in Singapore

eras: The archival photograph shows Boat Quay’s commercial riverfront, with boats and buildings closely connected to the water.
A major programme addressed pollution in the Singapore River and Kallang Basin. It involved relocating activities as well as cleaning water.
The decade-long cleanup changed the river’s condition and helped create opportunities for different waterfront uses.
An inherited river, a new setting
Older quays and waterfront buildings sit beside much later development. A cleaner landscape also records planning decisions and social change.

name: Venice
title: The canal endured. Everyday life changed.
deck: A familiar waterfront can hide profound change. Venice shows why visual continuity and social continuity are different things.
archiveTitle: The Grand Canal in a historical print
archiveType: Photochrom print · colour added during printing
modernTitle: The Grand Canal in present-day Venice
changed: The historic city’s functions have shifted, with tourism pressure and changes in residential and commercial use. Familiar facades do not mean unchanged lives.
persisted: Canals, bridges, and closely built islands continue to organise movement. The city and lagoon remain interdependent.
notice: Compare the water route and building edges. This pair suggests continuity of urban form, not proof that residents’ daily lives stayed the same.
eras: Island settlements developed within a lagoon landscape. Water shaped how places connected and where people could build.
Venice grew into a major maritime power. Its urban system connected islands through canals, bridges, and shared institutions.
The canal becomes a travel image
The photochrom print records a later view of the Grand Canal. Its colours belong to the printing process.
The inherited urban layout remains recognisable, while tourism, housing changes, and high water pose distinct challenges.

name: New York City
title: The waterfront stayed. The horizon rose.
deck: Lower Manhattan’s skyline changed through cycles of construction. The harbour view helps make that vertical transformation legible.
archiveTitle: Manhattan skyline from New Jersey
archiveType: Historical photograph · Library of Congress collection
changed: Office towers grew through advances in construction, elevators, and finance. Height emerged from economic and regulatory choices, not technology alone.
persisted: The waterfront still provides a way to read the skyline as a whole, even as individual buildings change.
notice: Look at the height and spacing of towers in the 1900 view. The newer photograph is another waterfront perspective, not an aligned repeat photograph.
eras: Clusters of taller office buildings began changing Manhattan’s profile. Valuable commercial land and new building techniques encouraged upward growth.
The archive photograph shows an earlier skyline across the water. New York was not a low-rise blank slate awaiting skyscrapers.
Construction booms filled Lower Manhattan with taller buildings. Foundations, steel frames, elevators, investment, and regulation all shaped the result.
The skyline contains buildings from different periods. Its identity comes from successive additions and replacements rather than one master design.

name: Hiroshima
title: A ruin preserved. A city rebuilt.
deck: The Atomic Bomb Dome connects destruction with deliberate remembrance. Its survival should be read within the history of the people and city around it.
archiveTitle: The damaged dome after the atomic bombing
modernTitle: The preserved Atomic Bomb Dome in 2018
changed: The surrounding city was rebuilt while the damaged dome was deliberately conserved. Preservation did not mean restoring the building to its original appearance.
persisted: The surviving structure provides physical testimony to the bombing and a focus for remembrance and peace.
notice: Both images show a damaged building, but their surroundings differ. The later landscape reflects a choice to preserve the ruin within a rebuilt city.

sources.name: Hiroshima City · The Story of the Atomic Bomb Dome

eras: The building began as a commercial exhibition hall on the Motoyasu River, designed to promote local products.
The atomic bombing on 6 August devastated Hiroshima. The hall was burned and severely damaged; part of its structure remained.
As the city recovered, debate over the ruin led to a deliberate policy of conservation rather than demolition or full reconstruction.
The preserved dome stands within a landscape of remembrance. It is evidence of destruction, not a substitute for the wider human story.

name: Seoul
title: A stream hidden. A stream revealed.
deck: Cheonggyecheon shows how the same corridor can serve very different ideas of a modern city.
archiveTitle: Construction covering Cheonggyecheon
changed: A covered watercourse and traffic corridor became a public space beside flowing water.
persisted: The stream’s route still threads through central Seoul, even as its surroundings and management change.
notice: The archive shows covering work, not the later elevated highway. Today’s stream is maintained infrastructure, rather than an untouched river.
eras: The stream formed a working corridor within the growing capital.
The archive catches the physical act of covering the channel. Later roads made traffic the dominant experience here.
Seoul removed road infrastructure and reopened the stream as part of a major restoration project.
Paths and crossings bring people close to the water. Its flow requires ongoing management and supplied water.

name: Hong Kong
title: The hills stayed. The shoreline moved.
deck: An early harbour painting and a modern skyline reveal both a recognisable setting and a waterfront rebuilt outward.
archiveTitle: Hong Kong Harbour and Victoria Peak
modernTitle: Victoria Harbour and the modern skyline
changed: Reclamation extended parts of the shore while successive development built upward.
persisted: The harbour and steep island backdrop continue to shape the city’s identity.
notice: Compare the hills and the density of buildings. These are different viewpoints, and the painted scene is an artist’s representation.

sources.name: Hong Kong Development Bureau · Our Central

eras: The area later known as Central developed as a colonial administrative and trading centre beside the harbour.
The archive painting records an early view of shipping and settlement beneath the island’s hills.
Reclamation, transport links, and rebuilding changed the relationship between streets and shore.
High-rise development defines much of the skyline, while the harbour remains the larger geographic frame.

name: Warsaw
title: An old town built again.
deck: Warsaw asks a surprising question: can a reconstructed place carry a city’s historical identity?
archiveTitle: The ruined Old Town Market Square, Barss side
modernTitle: Warsaw’s reconstructed Old Town Market Place
changed: Ruined buildings were reconstructed to recover the historic townscape.
persisted: The market square’s role as a recognisable civic place survived through deliberate rebuilding.
notice: The old appearance of the facades does not mean they passed through the war intact.
eras: Centuries of building had shaped the Old Town’s streets and market square.
Nazi forces devastated the historic centre. The archive shows the square in ruins after the war.
Residents and specialists reconstructed the historic urban form, including townhouses and public spaces.
The rebuilt centre is recognised by UNESCO. Its significance includes the collective decision to recover a lost townscape.

name: San Francisco
title: A city interrupted. A skyline rebuilt.
deck: A 1906 aerial panorama records the scale of destruction; a modern bay view shows a city whose story continued.
archiveTitle: San Francisco after the earthquake and fire
archiveType: Historical aerial photograph · George R. Lawrence
modernTitle: The modern San Francisco waterfront and Bay Bridge
changed: Rebuilding and later development transformed the skyline after the earthquake and fires.
persisted: The bay remains the setting in which the city’s growth is read.
notice: The archive is unusually wide. Look across the damaged urban fabric rather than treating it as a matching view of the modern bridge.

sources.name: Library of Congress · San Francisco panorama

eras: Dense neighbourhoods and commercial streets occupied the peninsula before the disaster.
The earthquake and the fires that followed devastated large areas of the city.
George R. Lawrence’s aerial photograph makes the extent of destruction visible across many blocks at once.
A rebuilt and expanded city faces the same bay. The modern view belongs to a later era of bridges and high-rise development.

name: Dubai
title: Before the skyline, the creek.
deck: Follow Dubai through the waterway that supported its trading life, rather than starting with its tallest buildings.
archiveTitle: Dubai Creek in the mid-1960s
modernTitle: Dubai Creek and its working waterfront
changed: Dredging, crossings, and urban growth altered how the creek served the city.
persisted: Boats and waterfront activity still make the creek a place of movement and exchange.
notice: The archive belongs to a city already trading and developing. It is not a picture of an empty desert before Dubai existed.

sources.name: UNESCO Tentative Lists · Khor Dubai · submitted by the UAE

eras: Fishing, pearling, and trade connected settlement around the creek to maritime routes.
Dredging improved access to the shallow creek and supported its commercial role.
The archive shows the creek during a period of infrastructure growth, rather than before all modern development.
Water transport and working vessels share the creek with visitor activity. Its older geography remains legible within a much larger city.

name: Canberra
title: A bridge waiting for its lake.
deck: A construction photograph reveals a familiar capital landmark before the water arrived.
archiveTitle: Kings Avenue Bridge under construction before the lake filled
modernTitle: Kings Avenue Bridge across Lake Burley Griffin
changed: A river floodplain became an artificial lake, reshaping views and movement through the capital.
persisted: The surrounding landforms remain the setting for the city’s planned axes and crossings.
notice: In the archive, bridge construction stands above dry ground. The modern view shows the completed crossing with the lake around it.

sources.name: National Capital Authority · Lake Burley Griffin

eras: A lake formed an important part of the design for the national capital. The design preceded its construction by decades.
The archive catches Kings Avenue Bridge being built while the future lake bed was still exposed.
Scrivener Dam’s valves closed in September 1963. After a dry interval, rain filled the lake in 1964.
The lake now frames national institutions, recreation areas, and bridges. Its level is managed by the dam.

name: Brasília
title: A capital drawn, then built.
deck: Construction on the Esplanade of Ministries gives a rare view of a capital city taking physical shape.
archiveTitle: Ministry buildings under construction in Brasília
changed: A construction landscape became the administrative heart of a new capital.
persisted: The relationship between monumental buildings, open space, and the city plan remains central to its identity.
notice: The archive belongs to the construction period. The finished city was made by workers and evolving decisions, not by a drawing alone.
eras: Brazil began creating a new capital in the country’s interior as part of a wider modernization project.
Lúcio Costa’s urban plan and Oscar Niemeyer’s major public buildings took shape. The archive shows ministry construction in 1959.
Brasília was inaugurated on 21 April 1960. The new administrative centre marked a major shift inland.
The protected modernist core is also a place of work and daily life. Its streets and buildings invite visitors to read the original planning ideas.

name: Mostar
title: A crossing lost. A crossing restored.
deck: The Old Bridge’s familiar arch carries a history of construction, destruction, and deliberate rebuilding.
archiveTitle: Mostar with the original Old Bridge over the Neretva
archiveType: Photochrom print · historical colours added in printing
changed: The original bridge was destroyed in 1993; the arch seen today is a reconstruction inaugurated in 2004.
persisted: The river crossing remains a defining element of the townscape and its memory.
notice: A similar arch appears in both views, but these are not images of the same surviving structure.

sources.name: UNESCO · Old Bridge Area of Mostar

eras: The stone bridge joined the banks of the Neretva and became a defining landmark of Mostar.
The archive print shows the old bridge before its twentieth-century destruction. Its colours were added during photochrom printing.
Shelling destroyed the bridge on 9 November 1993 during the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
International cooperation supported reconstruction of the bridge and its surroundings. The new bridge reopened in 2004; rebuilding also raised questions about memory and authenticity.

name: Rotterdam
title: Rebuilding without turning back.
deck: Rotterdam’s ruined centre and modern riverfront reveal a city whose reconstruction changed its urban form.
archiveTitle: Ruins of the Hoogstraat and surrounding streets
modernTitle: The Erasmus Bridge and modern Rotterdam
changed: Reconstruction replaced parts of the fine-grained centre with larger blocks, broader streets, and open spaces.
persisted: The city’s relationship with water remains visible, even as its buildings and crossings change.
notice: These views show different districts. The ruins explain the reconstruction context; the modern bridge is a later chapter, not a direct replacement for the street pictured.

sources.name: Dutch Cultural Heritage Agency · Rotterdam reconstruction

eras: The historic centre had a finer-grained street pattern than the reconstructed city that followed.
The bombing of 14 May destroyed much of the historic centre. The archive shows ruins around the Hoogstraat later that year.
Planning began soon after the bombing. Larger city blocks, broad boulevards, and generous green spaces reshaped the centre.
The modern riverfront adds another layer to the city. The comparison asks how a city can retain its identity while changing its physical form.

name: Valletta
title: A fortress with a life beyond defence.
deck: Harbour-side fortifications frame a capital whose everyday life extends far beyond its military origins.
archiveTitle: Lascaris Bastion and Upper Barrakka Gardens
modernTitle: Valletta and its fortified harbour setting
changed: A fortified capital has accumulated new civic, cultural, and visitor uses while retaining much of its historic form.
persisted: The bastions and peninsula setting still help explain the city’s shape.
notice: The archive is a nineteenth-century view of an older city. It does not show Valletta at its foundation in 1566.
eras: The Order of St John founded Valletta after the Great Siege of 1565, with defence central to its plan.
Religious, charitable, administrative, and residential buildings created a compact city within the fortifications.
The archive shows Lascaris Bastion and Upper Barrakka Gardens, bringing defensive masonry and public space into the same view.
The fortified form remains legible within a functioning capital. Streets, gardens, and public buildings connect daily life with the city’s older fabric.

name: Mexico City
title: The city beneath the city.
deck: A sixteenth-century map and an excavated temple reveal traces of Tenochtitlan in the modern capital.
archiveTitle: Printed map of Tenochtitlan
changed: The Mexica ceremonial centre was dismantled after the Spanish conquest, and colonial construction reshaped the area.
persisted: The historic centre still occupies part of the earlier city, whose remains can be seen at Templo Mayor.
notice: The map presents a historical interpretation of the lake city. The modern photograph shows one excavated site.

sources.name: New York Public Library · Map of Tenochtitlan

eras: Tenochtitlan was the political and religious centre of the Mexica. Templo Mayor stood at the heart of its sacred precinct.
A city on the printed page
Published after the Spanish conquest, the map depicts the island city and its links to the shore.
Utility workers found the Coyolxauhqui sculpture. The discovery prompted a wider archaeological project around Templo Mayor.
The excavation and museum let visitors encounter remains of the Mexica capital beside the buildings of today’s historic centre.

name: Cape Town
title: The neighborhood that was taken away.
deck: District Six tells a story of forced removal, community memory, and the long work of return.
archiveTitle: District Six after forced removals and demolition
changed: Apartheid authorities forced residents out and demolished much of the neighborhood.
persisted: Former residents and their families have kept the neighborhood’s history alive through testimony and community work.
notice: The archive shows the aftermath of clearance. The Homecoming Centre provides a different view of how the neighborhood is remembered.

sources.name: City of Cape Town · District Six heritage
South African History Archive · District Six

eras: District Six was home to a diverse community near the centre of Cape Town.
Under the Group Areas Act, the apartheid government designated District Six for white occupation.
Residents were displaced and much of the neighborhood was cleared. The archive photograph records the landscape decades later.
The District Six Museum draws on the memories of displaced residents and their families to document what was lost.

name: Bilbao
title: A river with a second working life.
deck: An older river crossing and today’s cultural waterfront show how Bilbao’s relationship with its estuary evolved.
archiveTitle: The Isabel II bridge and Bilbao’s historic riverfront
modernTitle: The Guggenheim Museum on the redeveloped waterfront
changed: Former industrial and port land at Abandoibarra became a district of public spaces, cultural institutions, and new buildings.
persisted: The estuary still links districts and provides a way to read the city’s development.
notice: The photographs show different parts of the same estuary. The old bridge view gives context for the waterfront’s earlier role.

sources.name: Lee Kuan Yew World City Prize · Abandoibarra waterfront

eras: The archive view shows a crossing connecting parts of a city organised around its waterway.
Port and industrial activity occupied land at Abandoibarra, near the city centre.
A new role for port land
Industrial decline opened former working sites to redevelopment. The museum became one part of a wider district plan.
Public spaces and cultural buildings now draw visitors to the estuary. The river remains the geographic thread.

name: Boston
title: The streets built over the tide.
deck: An 1852 plan shows Back Bay while its transformation from tidal flats to a neighborhood was still being planned.
archiveTitle: Plan of Back Bay and its vicinity
modernTitle: Boston’s Back Bay skyline from the Charles River
changed: Fill created land for a new street grid and buildings where tidal flats once extended.
persisted: The name Back Bay preserves a clue to the earlier landscape.
notice: Look for the water and proposed streets on the plan. Proposed lines show an intention, while the photograph looks toward the built neighborhood.

sources.name: National Park Service · Boston’s Green Connection

eras: The Back Bay area included tidal flats, marshes, and creeks.
The archive plan records a stage in the effort to turn the bay into buildable ground.
Filling extended the city onto land that had once been part of the bay.
The old geography in a name
Back Bay is now a built neighborhood. Its name and the historical map make the earlier shoreline easier to imagine.

name: Zanzibar City
title: A port written in stone.
deck: Stone Town’s waterfront gives a view into the Indian Ocean connections that shaped its buildings and streets.
archiveTitle: Exterior of the Sultan’s palace in Zanzibar
modernTitle: Stone Town in the modern city
changed: The old trading town became a protected historic district within a growing city.
persisted: The street pattern and architecture still show influences from across the Indian Ocean.
notice: The palace shows one side of port life. The wider story also includes enslaved people and the networks that profited from their trade.

sources.name: Library of Congress · Sultan’s palace photograph

eras: Trade connected Zanzibar to the East African coast and ports across the Indian Ocean.
The palace reflects the political importance of the port. Zanzibar’s trade also included the trafficking of enslaved people.
Buildings and the compact street pattern reflect encounters between Swahili, Arab, Indian, and European traditions.
Stone Town’s heritage is visible in its buildings and public spaces, within a city that continues to change.

name: Aswan & Abu Simbel
title: The temples that moved.
deck: The High Dam changed the Nile valley. At Abu Simbel, rescuers moved two temples above the rising water.
archiveTitle: Finishing work at the relocated Great Temple
modernTitle: Abu Simbel at its relocated site
changed: The reservoir covered parts of the old valley. Nubian communities were displaced, while selected monuments were relocated.
persisted: The temples still face the Nile landscape from their reconstructed setting.
notice: The archive shows work at the new site before inauguration.
eras: The temples of Abu Simbel were carved into the rock under Ramesses II.
Construction of the Aswan High Dam threatened monuments and displaced Nubian communities.
Workers cut the temples into blocks and rebuilt them higher above the valley.
The reconstructed setting preserves the monumental façades and gives visitors a view of the rescue work’s result.

name: Paris
title: An avenue through the old city.
deck: Avenue de l’Opéra shows how nineteenth-century rebuilding opened new routes and views through Paris.
archiveTitle: Streetlamp on Avenue de l’Opéra, photographed by Charles Marville
modernTitle: Avenue de l’Opéra in modern Paris
changed: A broad avenue cut through an older network of streets.
persisted: The avenue still frames the approach to the opera house.
notice: Marville’s close view shows the avenue’s street furniture. The wider modern photograph shows the corridor those lamps once lined.

sources.name: City of Paris · Haussmann and Marville

eras: Small streets and densely built blocks occupied the area crossed by the new avenue.
Under Napoleon III, Haussmann oversaw extensive changes to the capital’s streets and infrastructure.
Marville documented details of the rebuilt city, including this streetlamp on the avenue.
The broad street still leads the eye toward the Palais Garnier.

name: Medellín
title: When the hills joined the metro.
deck: A cable car made the steep slopes part of Medellín’s everyday transit network.
archiveTitle: An early view of Metrocable and Biblioteca España
changed: Line K connected hillside neighborhoods to the metro at Acevedo.
persisted: The slopes still shape the route, the station locations, and the view from each cabin.
notice: The archive shows the line in service several years after it opened.
eras: Hillside neighborhoods and valley transport corridors presented different access challenges.
Line K began service, linking the slopes with the rail network at Acevedo.
The archive shows the cable route alongside the Biblioteca España in Santo Domingo.
A transit network above the streets
Cable cars serve parts of the metropolitan network, connecting stations across terrain that shapes how people travel.

name: Detroit
title: A station finds a second life.
deck: Michigan Central Station went from rail gateway to long closure and then reopened with a new purpose.
archiveTitle: Postcard of the new Michigan Central Station
changed: Passenger rail service ended in 1988. The restored building reopened in 2024 as part of a technology and cultural campus.
persisted: The station’s prominent tower and grand entrance still anchor the view.
notice: Compare the tower and entrance. The modern image dates from shortly before the reopening.

sources.name: The Henry Ford · Michigan Central Station

eras: Michigan Central Station opened as a major passenger rail terminal.
The archive shows the new building as a landmark worth sending home.
The last passenger trains departed and the station entered a long period of vacancy.
Restoration gave the building a new role in a campus for technology and public events.

name: Wellington
title: The shoreline that moved.
deck: An early town plan records a harbour edge reshaped by earthquake uplift and later reclamation.
archiveTitle: Early plan of the town of Wellington
modernTitle: Wellington Harbour and the modern waterfront
changed: Earthquake uplift changed parts of the coast. Reclamation separately extended the built waterfront.
persisted: The harbour and steep hills still frame the city.
notice: Use the plan to locate the old shoreline. Proposed streets on the map show the surveyors’ intentions.

sources.name: Te Ara · Plans for Wellington in 1841
Wellington City Council · Old Shoreline Trail

eras: A town plan at the harbour
The early survey placed streets beside Lambton Harbour in a landscape already inhabited by Māori.
The Wairarapa earthquake lifted land around Wellington Harbour and altered parts of the shoreline.
Reclamation added land in stages, extending the waterfront beyond the earlier shoreline.
The modern waterfront lies beyond parts of the shore shown on early plans. The harbour remains central to the city’s shape.

name: Panama City
title: The city that moved.
deck: Two sites tell the story of a capital rebuilt on a different stretch of coast.
archiveTitle: Ruins of the original city at Panamá Viejo
modernTitle: Casco Antiguo, the relocated historic centre
changed: The city moved after the original settlement was destroyed in 1671.
persisted: The Pacific coast continued to shape the city’s role as a trading and administrative centre.
notice: The images show two separate sites. The ruined cathedral tower belongs to the original settlement.

sources.name: UNESCO · Archaeological Site and Historic Centre of Panamá City

eras: The Spanish founded Panamá at the site now called Panamá Viejo.
The attack led by Henry Morgan left the city devastated.
The settlement moved to a peninsula where it could be defended more readily.
Two places to read one history
The ruins of Panamá Viejo and the streets of Casco Antiguo preserve different chapters of the city’s development.

name: Barcelona
title: The city that grew into a grid.
deck: Cerdà’s expansion plan and the Eixample from above show how a drawing became a street pattern.
archiveTitle: Ildefons Cerdà’s expansion plan
changed: Expansion extended Barcelona beyond the old city in a regular network of streets and blocks.
persisted: The clipped block corners and diagonal routes remain easy to spot from above.
notice: Compare the repeated block shapes. The plan records Cerdà’s proposal, while the aerial view records what was built.

The city rebuilt with brick and stone, and street grades changed in parts of the district.
Pioneer Square preserves much of the streetscape built after the fire.

Street façades and decorative details let visitors read the period of reconstruction.

name: Chandigarh

The Capitol Complex brought together the Secretariat, Assembly, and High Court.
The complex remains a government precinct and part of a UNESCO listing for Le Corbusier’s architectural work.

Armed groups destroyed mausoleums that held religious and cultural significance for residents.
Local masons used traditional techniques to rebuild the mausoleums, with support from UNESCO and partners.

The old walls and the buildings of the expanding city reveal different periods of Baku’s history.

name: Pompeii

name: Athens

name: Edinburgh
